front: Which echocardiographic view is most sensitive for interatrial septum evaluation?
back: Subcostal 4-chamber view — the beam is perpendicular to the septum, minimizing drop-out.

front: Describe lipomatous hypertrophy of the atrial septum.
back: Non-encapsulated fatty infiltration of the interatrial septum with a characteristic 'dumbbell' shape that SPARES the fossa ovalis. Benign; can be very echogenic.

front: On agitated saline contrast study, within how many cardiac cycles must bubbles appear in the LA to suggest an intracardiac (PFO) shunt?
back: Within 3 cardiac cycles of RA opacification. Later appearance (> 3–5 beats) suggests an intrapulmonary shunt (e.g., pulmonary AVM in HHT).

front: State four types of ASD in order of frequency.
back: 1) Secundum (~75%, fossa ovalis). 2) Primum (inferior AV septum, associated with cleft AMVL). 3) Sinus venosus (SVC or IVC type, often with anomalous right PV drainage). 4) Coronary sinus (unroofed CS).
Excursion of the atrial septum > 10 mm into either atrium from the mid-septal plane, or 15 mm total excursion. Associated with PFO and cryptogenic stroke.

front: Which type of VSD is most likely to lead to progressive aortic regurgitation, and why?
back: Supracristal (outlet / subpulmonary / infundibular) VSD — the defect sits below the pulmonic valve near the aortic annulus. Right coronary cusp of the AV prolapses into the defect over time, leading to AR.
A congenital or acquired shunt from the LV to the RA through the membranous IVS, above the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve. Rare complication of endocarditis, MI, or congenital heart disease.

front: Describe septal motion after cardiac surgery.
back: Paradoxical septal motion toward the RV in systole, with PRESERVED normal thickening. From translational motion of the heart (post-op adhesions/altered geometry), not true dysfunction.

front: Sinus venosus ASD is most commonly associated with what pulmonary vein anomaly?
back: Anomalous drainage of the right upper pulmonary vein (partial anomalous pulmonary venous return — PAPVR), typically into the SVC.

front: Most common type of VSD overall and its typical closure tendency?
back: Perimembranous VSD is most common overall. Muscular VSDs (particularly small ones) close spontaneously most often. Perimembranous defects may partially close by TV septal leaflet coverage ('windsock' or aneurysm formation).
